name: Dentist take-home whitening trays

card.summary: Custom-fitted trays loaded with dentist-supplied peroxide gel and worn at home; gentler on sensitivity than in-office bleaching, with modest shade gains.
card.note: Poorly fitting trays are linked to gum burns; stains can return within months.

quick.overview:
These are trays moulded to the user's teeth by a dentist and filled with carbamide peroxide gel, worn at home for a few hours or overnight. Custom tray bleaching dates back to the late 1960s and was popularised by a 1989 paper by Haywood and Heymann.

Wikipedia describes shade gains of about 1 to 2 shades within several days with trays, and says home-based bleaching produces less sensitivity than in-office bleaching. Effects fade, and retreatment every six to twelve months is mentioned.
quick.mechanism: Carbamide peroxide releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water, generating free radicals that break down pigment molecules in the tooth. A custom fit is said to keep gel against the teeth and reduce leakage onto the gums.
quick.risks: Sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects; chemical burns often follow poorly fitting trays, and peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage tissue. Listed contraindications include age under 16, pregnancy, untreated decay or gum disease, and exposed dentine.

lead: Dentist take-home whitening trays are custom-fitted trays, made from an impression of the teeth, that hold peroxide gel against the teeth while worn at home. People use them to lighten stained or yellowed teeth for a brighter smile, with the dentist supplying the tray and gel and supervising the process. Carbamide peroxide, which breaks down to hydrogen peroxide in the mouth, is the usual agent [1].

Wikipedia reports that, following manufacturer instructions, trays worn overnight or for two to four hours a day can lighten teeth by one or two shades within about three days, and that home bleaching causes less tooth sensitivity than in-office bleaching [1]. A dentist-made tray can take up to a week to produce, and can later be reused for maintenance top-ups [1]. A custom fit reduces gel leakage onto the gums, whereas poorly fitting trays are among the most common causes of chemical burns [1].

A 2018 Cochrane review of home-based bleaching reported low to very low certainty evidence that it works better than placebo over periods from two weeks to six months, and found tooth sensitivity and oral irritation to be the most common side effects, mild, transient and more frequent at higher concentrations [2]. Colour can rebound as teeth rehydrate and stains can return within months [1].
infobox: Up to 6% hydrogen peroxide or 16% carbamide peroxide [1]

paras: Wikipedia credits Dr William Klusmeier with introducing custom tray bleaching in the late 1960s [1]. In 1989 Haywood and Heymann published support for custom trays, with carbamide peroxide favoured for a shelf life of one to two years versus one to two months for hydrogen peroxide [1].

Trays are described as worn overnight or for 2 to 4 hours daily, with 1 to 2 shades lightening reported within about three days [1]. Stains can return within a few months, and brushing or rinsing after food and drink, flossing and avoiding staining foods for 24 to 48 hours are among the maintenance steps listed [1].

Wikipedia describes post-whitening sensitivity as lasting about 4 to 39 days depending on the person, and notes that inconsistent use slows and makes whitening patchy [1]. Colour can rebound as teeth rehydrate, particularly where much of the immediate change came from dehydration [1].

Wikipedia describes strips (typically twice daily for 30 minutes over 14 days), brush-on gels (twice daily for 14 days), rinses (twice daily for a minute, with improvement over up to three months) and whitening toothpastes with low peroxide levels, each giving about one or two shades of change [1].

Sensitivity is reported with whitening generally, and potassium nitrate and fluoride toothpastes ease it without evidence that they prevent it permanently [1]. Peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage gum tissue [1].

In the EU, retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6 percent allowed under professional supervision [1]. The US FDA is cited as endorsing gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide [1].

Wikipedia also notes that people with a strong gag reflex may not tolerate trays, and that erratic or inaccurate use can cause blistering, sensitivity or soft-tissue irritation [1]. The Cochrane review reported sensitivity and oral irritation as the most common side effects [2].

The 2018 Cochrane review of home-based chemically-induced whitening of teeth in adults (an update of a 2006 version) reported low to very low certainty evidence of effectiveness against placebo over two weeks to six months, and could not establish whether any particular composition, concentration or application time was superior [2]. Wikipedia cites a 2014 review by Carey on tooth whitening and a 2007 14-day trial by Delgado and colleagues of custom-tray 9% hydrogen peroxide and 20% carbamide peroxide [1].

timeline.event: Custom tray bleaching introduced by Dr William Klusmeier.[1]
Haywood and Heymann publish support for custom trays.[1]
Cochrane review of home-based tooth bleaching published [2].

angle.text: People wear dentist-fitted trays loaded with peroxide gel to lighten teeth by a shade or two for a brighter smile. A snug custom fit keeps gel on the teeth and off the gums.
